final_answer:
Short answer: the District of South Carolina (Fourth Circuit) is the better office to bring the single, consolidated indictment, with the caveat that the guidelines themselves make the choice of district matter far less than the choice to prosecute everything in ONE case. Confidence is moderate, and the South Carolina preference rests on a circuit-law point that has been largely mooted by a 2024 guideline amendment.

1. Why a single indictment matters most. Section 1347 offenses are 'offenses of a character for which USSG 3D1.2(d) would require grouping' (2B1.1 is on the 3D1.2(d) list). Under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2), the offense level therefore includes all acts that were part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan as the offense of conviction, whether or not charged and regardless of the state or district in which they occurred. So one office that charges (or merely proves as relevant conduct) the claims in both states gets a single loss total from both states, a single 2B1.1 offense level, and, if the loss exceeds $1 million and involves a government health care program (Medicare/Medicaid), the 2B1.1(b)(7) enhancement. Multiple counts group under 3D1.2(d), so the Guidelines range reflects aggregate loss rather than a separate, lower range for each state. If instead each office prosecutes separately, the second sentencing court still counts the first-state conduct as relevant conduct (inflating its own range), but USSG 5G1.3(b) then directs the second sentence to run concurrently to the earlier sentence to the extent the earlier offense was relevant conduct that increased the offense level, and 5G1.3(d)/(c) give discretion otherwise. Separate prosecutions therefore risk overlapping, concurrent time, defeating the goal of maximizing imprisonment. Also, each office is limited by venue: a district may charge only offenses committed in whole or part there (U.S. Const. art. III, sec. 2; Sixth Amendment; 18 U.S.C. 3237(a)), so a district can charge the other state's claims only if venue exists (e.g., a single scheme with acts, mailings, or electronic submissions in that district, or a conspiracy count). I could not verify venue facts and they are unknown; if only one office has venue over the cross-border claims, that office is the only one that can reach everything in one indictment.

2. Statutory ceiling. Each 1347 count carries a 10-year maximum (20 years if serious bodily injury results; any term of years or life if death results), 18 U.S.C. 1347(a). With a guideline range driven by aggregate loss, many counts allow the court to stack under USSG 5G1.2(d) to reach the total punishment. (I could not fetch the statute text; stated from knowledge, not verified in this run.)

3. Which district. Both districts follow the Guidelines, but appellate law differs on how loss is measured. Southern District of Georgia sits in the Eleventh Circuit, where United States v. Dupree, 57 F.4th 1269 (11th Cir. 2023) (en banc), holds that Kisor deference to Guidelines commentary applies only if the guideline text is genuinely ambiguous and so commentary cannot expand a guideline; this led Eleventh Circuit courts to reject the commentary's 'intended loss' rule for 2B1.1 and to limit loss to actual loss, which can lower the range in fraud cases where claims were denied or not paid. The District of South Carolina sits in the Fourth Circuit, where United States v. Boler, 115 F.4th 316 (4th Cir. 2024), found 'loss' ambiguous and allowed deference to the commentary's 'greater of actual or intended loss.' Billed-but-unpaid false claims therefore count more readily in South Carolina. Caveat: the Commission's 2024 amendment (effective Nov. 1, 2024) moved the intended-loss definition into the guideline text of 2B1.1, which substantially eliminates this split for sentences under the current Manual, so the advantage is modest and applies mainly if the Manual in effect or the ex post facto-limited version at sentencing is pre-amendment. I verified the case holdings only through search summaries and did not verify the amendment's text in this run.

4. Practical tie-breakers: (a) whichever district has venue over, and evidence for, the larger share of the loss and government-program claims should lead, since the other state's claims enter as relevant conduct; (b) whichever can reach all the conduct through one scheme or conspiracy count; (c) circuit law above favors South Carolina; (d) coordinate so only one office indicts, to avoid 5G1.3 concurrency and sequencing problems. Because the facts give no loss split, the recommendation is South Carolina on the circuit-law basis, subject to venue and loss facts.
